FLORIDA / TRIP PLANNING

Florida visitor fishing license planner

Florida visitors aged 16 or older usually need a fishing license, even for catch and release. A properly licensed saltwater charter or pier can cover that outing. Use this planner to separate those trips from beach, private-boat, and freshwater fishing before you choose your license.

By Castward Updated 12 November 2026

Quick answer

Start with the trip, not the cheapest license. A visitor cannot use Florida’s free resident shoreline license. Confirm charter or pier coverage with the operator; buy personal coverage for separate shore or private-boat outings. Freshwater trips need their own check. Species permits and catch rules can still apply.[1] [2] [3]

01

Which license fits your Florida outing?

Choose the activity for one outing. Run it again if your plans change. The result covers the basic license decision, not permission to keep a particular fish.[2] [1] [4] [3]

Choose your outing, then check the result. The table below also works without JavaScript.

For Florida visitors. This tool does not decide species permits, open seasons, local access, or every special exemption. Check FWC before you fish.

03

Should you choose three days, seven days, or a year?

FWC lists nonresident saltwater base fees of $17 for three days, $30 for seven days, and $47 for one year. Additional handling fees can apply. Match the license dates to the actual fishing outings, not just the hotel stay.

For a four-day visit with fishing on the first and last day, compare a seven-day license with the dates offered at checkout. A three-day period will not span both outings. An annual license can be worth comparing if you expect another visit.[4]

Swipe the table to compare all columns.

Saltwater optionListed base fee (USD)Planning use

7-day$30Several outings across a week
Annual$47Longer stays or repeat visits
04

What changes when you fish twice on the same holiday?

Example: you book a saltwater charter for Tuesday and want to cast from the beach on Thursday. Ask the captain about Tuesday’s coverage. Treat Thursday as a new license decision; the charter’s coverage does not follow you onto the beach.

Example: a family visits a saltwater pier. Check the pier’s license with the operator before anyone casts. For children under 16, the age exemption applies, but species rules still matter. An adult who helps take fish should check their own coverage rather than assume the child’s exemption extends to them.[2] [3]

  • ✓Write down every planned fishing outing.
  • ✓Mark each outing as freshwater or saltwater.
  • ✓Ask the pier or charter operator about coverage.
  • ✓Choose personal coverage for outings that remain uncovered.
  • ✓Keep the issued license and the relevant rules accessible.
05

What can you still need beyond the basic license?

Check the exact target species before you cast. FWC lists separate requirements for activities such as snook or lobster harvest, specified reef fish from private vessels, and shore-based shark fishing. A basic license result is not a species-permit result.[4]

06

Can visitors use a license-free fishing day?

Yes. FWC includes residents and nonresidents in its recreational license-free days. Freshwater and saltwater use different calendars. Seasons, size limits, and bag limits still apply. Check the official date before you build a trip around the waiver.[5]

Swipe the table to compare all columns.

WaterFWC calendar rule
FreshwaterFirst consecutive Saturday and Sunday in April; second consecutive Saturday and Sunday in June.
SaltwaterFirst consecutive Saturday and Sunday in June; first Saturday in September; Saturday after Thanksgiving.
07

Where should you buy the license?

Use FWC’s official purchase route. It lists Go Outdoors Florida, license agents, tax collectors, its telephone service, and the Fish|Hunt FL app. If the short-term option you need is absent online, contact a listed agent before you travel. Do not replace it with a resident license.[6]

  • ✓Confirm the license type and start date before payment.
  • ✓Check the full checkout total, including any handling fee.
  • ✓Save the issued license where you can show it without a reliable signal.
  • ✓Recheck your route if the captain changes the trip or you add a shore session.
A few good questions

Before you head out

Can a visitor get the free Florida shoreline license?

No. That license is for Florida residents. Visitors need regular nonresident saltwater coverage unless an exemption applies.

Does catch and release need a license?

Yes, unless you qualify for an exemption. The license rule covers the attempt to take fish, not only fish you keep.

Does every Florida pier cover my license?

No. Ask the operator whether that pier has a current saltwater pier license that covers your outing.

Does a charter license cover beach fishing the next day?

No. Check the separate beach outing. The charter coverage does not become a personal holiday license.

Do visitors aged 65 or older fish free?

Florida’s age-65 senior exemption is for residents. Visiting seniors must check normal nonresident coverage and any other applicable exemption.

Do children under 16 need the basic fishing license?

FWC exempts children under 16. They must still follow the fishery rules.

Can I use this tool for a freshwater trip?

Use the freshwater result to reach the official Florida reference. This tool quotes saltwater fees only and does not treat a freshwater guide as a licensed saltwater charter.
